claims.claim: Anscombe's sets I to III share mean 7.50, variance about 4.12 to 4.13 and correlation 0.816.
claims.source: Anscombe (1973), The American Statistician 27(1); computed with NumPy 2.4.6 in this repository.

concept_html:
Summary statistics hide shape. Anscombe's quartet (1973) is four small datasets with the same means, variances and correlation. Computed in this course's build for the first three:

Set mean of y variance of y correlation with x
I 7.50 4.13 0.816
II 7.50 4.13 0.816
III 7.50 4.12 0.816

Plotted, set I is a noisy line, set II is a curve, and set III is a perfect line with one outlier. The numbers alone cannot tell them apart.

Four plots catch most problems:

  • Histogram of each key numeric column. Shows skew, gaps, spikes at codes such as 99 or 0, and more than one peak.
  • Scatter plot of each pair you will model or correlate. Shows curves, clusters and single points that drive a correlation.
  • Line over time of counts and key rates by wave. Shows breaks in the series when a questionnaire or supplier changed.
  • Bar chart of missingness by column and by subgroup.

Make each plot honest:

  • Label both axes with units, and give every figure a title that states what it shows.
  • Choose histogram bins on purpose. Too few hide a spike at 99. Try two or three bin counts.
  • Use a log scale for heavily skewed values such as spend, and say so on the axis.
  • Plot the raw data before you plot the smoothed or aggregated version.

Write plotting code as functions that return a matplotlib.figure.Figure (matplotlib 3.10). Build with fig, ax = plt.subplots(), not the global plt.plot() state. A function that returns a figure is testable: a test reads ax.get_xlabel() or counts the bars. The caller decides whether to show it or save it.

lines: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.figure import Figure
def plot_distribution(values: list[float], title: str, xlabel: str, bins: int = 30) -> Figure:
"""Histogram of values with labelled axes. The caller shows or saves it."""
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.hist(values, bins=bins)
ax.set_title(title)
ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
ax.set_ylabel("Respondents")
return fig

exercises.solution:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.figure import Figure


def plot_distribution(values: list[float], title: str, xlabel: str, bins: int = 30) -> Figure:
    """Histogram of values with labelled axes.

    Args:
        values: Numbers to plot.
        title: Figure title.
        xlabel: X axis label, with units.
        bins: Number of histogram bins.

    Returns:
        The figure. The caller shows or saves it.
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    ax.hist(values, bins=bins)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Respondents")
    return fig

title: Plot before you summarise
why_html: A team reported a correlation of 0.62 between ad recall and purchase intent across 40 markets, and the client planned a budget shift on it. A scatter plot showed 39 markets in a flat cloud and one market far in the top-right corner. Without that market the correlation was close to zero. The decision was about one market, not 40.
